title: Concrete Is a Recipe With a Contract Attached
summary: Concrete's strength and durability are set by its recipe, above all by the ratio of water to cementing material, and then by how it is placed, covered and cured. The specification turns that recipe into a contract, and testing is how you prove the contract was met. Learn the water-cement ratio, exposure and cover, and most concrete arguments become simple.
body:
Concrete is a recipe that becomes rock, and the single number that decides most of its strength and its life is the ratio of water to cementing material, so the person who controls the water on the truck controls the building.

Recall

Q. What is a non-conformance report on a pile?

A. A written record that a pile does not meet its criteria, with the engineer's evaluation and the resolution, closed before the cap is poured over it.

Q. In shallow foundations, why can a footing be safe in bearing and still be a problem?

A. Because bearing capacity measures shear failure, while settlement measures movement under service load, and excessive or uneven settlement can damage the building long before the soil fails.

Q. Name the four control layers of a building envelope.

A. Water, air, vapour and thermal control. Each must be continuous, and the joints between materials are where they usually fail.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, concrete is probably the largest single material on a typical mid-rise building, and it is bought by the truckload from a supplier who mixes it to a recipe you approved months earlier. Every structural assumption Bram made, every fire rating Magnus relied on and every durability promise in your pro forma rests on that recipe arriving as approved and being placed properly. Most concrete failures are not exotic chemistry. They are water added to make the concrete easier to place, cover too thin over the steel, or curing skipped on a hot day. All three are decisions made by people on site, and all three are invisible once the concrete hardens.

Water and cement: the core relationship

In plain English: cement reacts with water to form the glue that binds sand and stone. It needs some water to react. Any extra water makes the mix flow more easily, but when that extra water leaves, it leaves tiny pores behind. More pores mean weaker concrete and an easier path for water and salt to reach the steel.

The professional measure is the water-cementitious materials ratio, written w/cm: the weight of water divided by the weight of all cementing materials, which includes cement and supplementary materials such as fly ash, slag cement and silica fume. A lower ratio gives higher strength and lower permeability, up to the point where the mix is too stiff to place well without admixtures.

Applied example, hypothetical round numbers. A mix contains 600 pounds of cementing material and 270 pounds of water per cubic yard. The w/cm is 270 divided by 600, which is 0.45. If a driver adds 10 gallons of water at site to loosen the mix, that is about 83 pounds of water, since a gallon of water weighs about 8.34 pounds. Water becomes 353 pounds, and w/cm becomes 353 divided by 600, which is about 0.59. The concrete that leaves the chute is no longer the concrete you approved. Its strength will be lower and its permeability higher, and the cylinders, if they are made from a sample taken before the water went in, will not show it.

Strength, exposure and cover

Specified compressive strength, written f prime c, is the strength the structural engineer designed for, usually measured on standard cylinders at 28 days and stated in pounds per square inch, psi. It is a design number, not a target average; the mix must be proportioned to average comfortably above it, because concrete varies. You will see that arithmetic on Day 5.

Exposure class is how the concrete code describes what the concrete will face: freezing and thawing, sulfate in soil or water, contact with water, or chlorides that corrode steel, such as seawater, salt spray and de-icing salts. Each class sets limits, such as a maximum w/cm and a minimum strength. A balcony over the sea and an interior column in a dry building are not the same concrete, even if they share a strength. Verify the classes and their limits against the current adopted edition of ACI 318.

Cover is the thickness of concrete between the reinforcing steel and the surface. It protects the steel from corrosion and from fire. Cover is specified by the engineer and checked before the pour. Applied example, hypothetical: a specification calls for 2 inches of cover on an exposed slab edge. Bar supports, called chairs, are installed at 1.5 inches. Half an inch sounds small. But chlorides reach steel through cover by diffusion, and the time to reach the steel rises roughly with the square of the cover depth, so losing a quarter of the cover can take away a large share of the time before corrosion starts. That is why cover is inspected with a tape, not assumed.

Say that out loud now.

Hot weather and cylinders

Heat speeds the reaction, shortens the working time, increases water demand and evaporation, and invites crews to add water. Hot-weather concreting practice, described in ACI 305, uses cooler materials, retarding admixtures, evening or early pours, windbreaks and prompt curing. The specification should set a maximum concrete temperature at placement and say what happens when it is exceeded.

Cylinder testing is how you prove strength. A technician samples concrete at the point of placement, makes cylinders under ASTM C31, and the laboratory breaks them under ASTM C39 at specified ages. Cylinders tell you what the delivered concrete could achieve under standard curing. They do not tell you about water added after sampling, missing cover or poor curing in place. That gap is why inspection and batch tickets matter as much as breaks.

How the best do it

Well-run projects hold a pre-construction concrete meeting with the structural engineer, the supplier, the placing contractor, the testing laboratory and the inspector, before the first structural pour. They agree the mixes by location, the slump and temperature limits, who may authorise water at site and how it is recorded, the sampling plan, and what happens on a low break. What a small developer can copy is the meeting itself and its minutes. It costs a morning and prevents most of the disputes this week will describe.

Who controls each variable

One practical map, Mr Shabazz. The engineer controls the specification: strength, exposure class, w/cm limit and cover. The supplier controls the recipe and the plant: materials, proportions and the batch ticket. The placing contractor controls the chute, the pump, the vibrator and the finishing. The rebar crew controls the chairs that set cover. The inspector and the laboratory control the evidence. When you know who controls each variable, you know whom to ask when a number looks wrong, and you can see at once when one party is making a decision that belongs to another.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is uncontrolled water at site, which silently lowers strength and durability. The control is a written rule: no water added beyond what the approved mix allows, only by a named person, recorded on the batch ticket, with sampling after any addition.

The beginner's mistake

Treating strength as the whole specification. Two mixes with the same strength can have very different durability, because exposure limits, cover and curing decide how long the steel stays safe.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: concrete and repair costs are treated differently depending on whether they create or restore an asset; ask your tax adviser, and verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: durability defects surface years later, so warranties and limitation periods must reach that far. Banking: the lender's monitor will ask for test reports before certifying structural progress. Governance: any mix substitution is an owner decision logged with the engineer's approval. Estate: a building whose concrete is documented is easier to hold or pass on. Exit: buyers' engineers test cover and chlorides, and poor results come straight off the price.

Callback

In Week 99, Ravi and Bram taught that salt air corrodes reinforcing steel and that exposure classes in the concrete code set limits for it. This week turns that rule into a recipe and a site check: a low ratio, the right class, and cover that is measured before the pour.

Recap

The water-cementitious ratio governs strength and permeability. Exposure class sets the limits for each location. Cover protects the steel and must be measured. Heat raises the temptation to add water. Cylinders prove the delivered mix, not the placed concrete.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: a composite coastal parking deck that corroded early.
checklist: I know the w/cm, strength and exposure class for each concrete location.
The specification states who may add water at site, how much, and how it is recorded.
Cover is checked with a tape before every pour, not assumed.
The specification sets a maximum concrete temperature at placement.
I hold a pre-construction concrete meeting with every party and keep minutes.
The sampling plan says where and when cylinders are taken.
Mix substitutions need the structural engineer's written approval.
Professional sign-off required: structural engineer of record and testing laboratory.

In a hypothetical mix, 270 pounds of water on 600 of cementing material is 0.45. Ten gallons added at site, about 83 pounds, takes it to about 0.59, and if the cylinders were sampled before the water went in, they will not show it. terms: Water-cementitious materials ratio (w/cm) — the weight of mixing water divided by the weight of cement and other cementing materials in a concrete mix.
Specified compressive strength — the design strength of concrete, usually measured on standard cylinders at 28 days, written f prime c.
Exposure class — the concrete code's category for what concrete will face, which sets limits such as maximum w/cm and minimum strength.

hostile.q: I'm the placing foreman. The mix is too stiff to pump today. Let me add water or we lose the pour.
hostile.a: No water beyond what the approved mix allows. If the mix is too stiff, the supplier can adjust with the approved water-reducing admixture, dosed and recorded at the plant or by their technician on the batch ticket, and the inspector samples after the adjustment. If that cannot happen, we stop the pour at a planned joint and finish tomorrow. A lost morning is cheap. Concrete with an unknown water ratio in the slab is not.

role: Failure forensics, with Cole on audit and integrity
title: The Parking Deck That Rusted From the Inside
summary: A composite case: a coastal parking structure built with a mix that met its strength but not its exposure limits, water added at site, and thin cover, began spalling within a few years of completion. Seven forensic steps show how each small departure compounded. The repair cost far exceeded the savings.
body:
This is a composite example: a parking deck near the sea passed every cylinder test and still began to rust from the inside within a few years, because the concrete that mattered was not the concrete that was tested.

Recall

Q. What does the w/cm ratio measure?

A. The weight of mixing water divided by the weight of all cementing materials. Lower ratios mean higher strength and lower permeability.

Q. What is dewatering, and why does it matter to neighbours?

A. Pumping groundwater down to keep an excavation dry. It increases effective stress in the soil and can cause soft layers under nearby buildings to settle.

Q. What is vapour drive in a building envelope?

A. The movement of water vapour through materials from the warmer, wetter side toward the cooler, drier side, which in hot-humid climates runs from outside to inside.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole joins me today because this case is about evidence. Every record said the deck was fine. The cylinders passed. The inspector's reports said the pours were complete. Only when the concrete started cracking off the slab soffits did anyone go back to the batch tickets, measure the cover and test chloride levels in the concrete. This is a composite example, built from patterns that recur in parking structures in salt environments. The numbers are hypothetical.

1. Timeline

A developer builds a multi-level cast-in-place parking structure a few hundred feet from the coast, serving a residential building. The specification calls for a mix with a maximum w/cm of 0.40 and 2 inches of cover on the top reinforcing of the decks, consistent with the engineer's chloride exposure classification. During procurement, a lower-priced supplier is substituted, and its submittal shows a mix with a w/cm of 0.45, accepted by the contractor's office without the engineer's sign-off because its strength matches. Pours run through a hot summer. Water is added at site on many trucks to help pumping. Within a few years of completion, rust stains and cracks appear on the deck soffits near drains and expansion joints. By year 8, sections of concrete are spalling, meaning breaking away, and exposing corroded steel.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions mattered. Accepting a mix submittal on strength alone. Tolerating water added at site without recording it. And signing off the decks without a cover survey before or after the pours.

3. Assumptions

The team assumed that a mix meeting strength met the specification. It assumed passing cylinders meant good concrete in place. And it assumed that cover set by the rebar crew was cover delivered, when chairs had been crushed by foot traffic and hoses during placement.

4. Incentives

The substituted supplier was cheaper. The placing crew was paid by the job and wanted faster pumping. The contractor wanted the deck finished before the hot season peaked. Nobody on site was rewarded for durability, because durability shows up years after everyone has been paid. Cole's point: when the incentive for a defect is immediate and the cost is delayed, only a documented check catches it.

Say that out loud now.

5. Warning signs ignored

The batch tickets recorded water added on site, in the driver's handwriting, on many trucks. Nobody read them. The inspector noted in daily reports that chairs were displaced in places. The mix submittal's w/cm was above the specification limit on its face. Early hairline cracking near drains was dismissed as shrinkage. Any one of these, read at the time, would have triggered a review.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was each pour itself. Once concrete with a high water ratio and thin cover hardened over the steel, the only remedies were costly: surface sealers to slow chloride entry, cathodic protection, or removal and replacement of concrete around corroded bars. Before each pour, the fixes were a rejected submittal, a turned-away truck and a re-set chair.

7. Root cause

The root cause was a quality system that measured strength and ignored durability. The specification held the right limits, but the submittal review, the site water control and the cover check that should have enforced them were either skipped or unread. The concrete passed the test it was given and failed the one that mattered.

The cost of the shortcut

Hypothetical figures. The substituted supplier saved perhaps 5 dollars per cubic yard on 6,000 cubic yards: 30,000 dollars. The repair programme in year 8, including concrete removal, new steel where needed, a deck coating and closures of parking levels, cost several million dollars, plus lost parking revenue, a dispute over who paid, and residents unhappy with a structure closed in sections. The ratio between saving and cost is the entire lesson.

What Cole would have checked

Cole's audit list, Mr Shabazz, for any concrete in a salt environment. One: every mix submittal reviewed and stamped by the structural engineer, with w/cm and exposure class checked against the specification, not only strength. Two: batch tickets collected for every truck and reviewed weekly for water added, time from batching to placement and concrete temperature. Three: a cover survey before every pour by the inspector, with photographs, and a cover-meter survey of finished decks on a sample basis. Four: early cracking near drains and joints logged and assessed by the engineer within the warranty period, not dismissed. None of these is expensive. All of them produce records that would have stopped this case, or at least moved its cost onto the parties who caused it.

Who should have paid

Cole's second point, Mr Shabazz, is about where the cost landed. In this composite, the owner discovered the problem after the contractor's warranty had expired, the supplier had been paid years earlier, and the records that could have shifted the cost were scattered or lost. So the owner paid most of the repair, and then spent more on lawyers trying to recover it. A different owner, holding the same facts, would have had three things in hand. A specification that made durability, not just strength, a contract requirement. A complete file of submittals, batch tickets, cover surveys and test results, indexed by pour. And a latent defect provision and limitation period that reached far enough to cover corrosion, which by its nature appears late.

The lesson is not that defects can always be passed to someone else. It is that the party holding the evidence decides where the cost settles. An owner with an organised file negotiates. An owner without one absorbs. Professional sign-off required: construction lawyer, for latent defect provisions and limitation periods, and verify those periods against the primary source before you rely on them.

The same pattern elsewhere

The parking deck is the clearest example because salt is relentless, but the pattern repeats on balconies, podium roofs, pool decks and foundation walls in wet ground. Any element that is wet, salted or both, and whose reinforcing steel sits close to the surface, is a candidate. When you walk a set of drawings, ask the engineer to point at every one of them and tell you its exposure class. If the answer is the same class everywhere, ask why.

A last forensic habit, Mr Shabazz: when you inherit or buy a building, ask for this file before you ask for the rent roll. Its absence is information. A seller who cannot produce the concrete records for exposed elements is asking you to price the risk yourself, and you should.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a quality system that reports green on strength while durability fails silently. The control is a durability checklist: approved w/cm, exposure class, recorded water, measured cover, and curing, each with a record.

The beginner's mistake

Believing the cylinder report settles the question. It settles one question about the delivered mix.

Callback

In Week 82, Vera taught that records nobody reads are not controls. The batch tickets here held the evidence from the first week of pours. The failure was not missing records; it was unread ones.

Recap

A composite parking deck met strength and failed durability: a substituted mix above the w/cm limit, unrecorded site water, thin cover. Small savings bought large repairs. Rule 112 makes durability evidence a condition of every pour.

Next: Sage, on The Money: what concrete durability costs, and what it saves.
checklist: Every mix submittal is reviewed by the structural engineer for w/cm and exposure, not only strength.
Mix substitutions are rejected unless the engineer approves in writing.
I collect and review batch tickets for water added, time and temperature.
The inspector measures and photographs cover before every pour.
A sample cover-meter survey checks finished concrete in exposed areas.
Early cracking near drains and joints is assessed by the engineer within warranty.
Curing is specified, observed and recorded.
Professional sign-off required: structural engineer of record and special inspector.
head: Field checklist
speak: This is a composite case. A coastal parking deck was specified at a maximum water-cementitious ratio of 0.40 with 2 inches of cover. A cheaper supplier's mix at 0.45 was accepted on strength alone, water was added at site to help pumping, and chairs were crushed during placement, thinning the cover. The cylinders passed. Within a few years rust stains appeared, and by year 8 concrete was spalling. The warning signs were on the batch tickets and in the inspector's notes, unread. The root cause was a quality system that measured strength and ignored durability. A saving of perhaps 30,000 dollars bought a repair of several million. Rule 112: no pour proceeds without evidence of the approved water ratio, the right exposure class and measured cover, and no water is added at site unless it is allowed, authorised and recorded.
terms: Spalling — concrete breaking away from a surface, often because corroding steel beneath it expands.
Batch ticket — the delivery record for each truck of concrete, showing the mix, quantities, times and any water added.
Cover meter — an instrument that locates reinforcing steel and estimates its depth below the concrete surface without breaking it.

hostile.q: I'm the insurer. Your parking deck is spalling after eight years. Why is that a construction defect rather than wear and tear?
hostile.a: Because the records show it. The specification required a maximum water ratio of 0.40 and 2 inches of cover for chloride exposure. The approved submittal shows 0.45 without the engineer's stamp, the batch tickets record water added at site on many trucks, and the cover survey shows large areas under specification. Chloride testing at the steel depth is consistent with that. Ordinary wear does not produce corrosion this early in concrete built as specified. I can give you the full file.

rule: Rule 112: No pour proceeds without evidence of the approved water-cementitious ratio, the right exposure class and measured cover, and no water is added at site unless the approved mix allows it, a named person authorises it and the batch ticket records it.

title: What Durability Costs, and What It Saves
summary: A better concrete mix and more cover cost a little more on day one and save large repair bills, closures and value losses later. The way to see it is to price both sides: the premium now, and the repair and lost income avoided, discounted to today. Durability is a valuation decision, not only a materials one.
body:
Durability is one of the cheapest value protections a developer can buy, because the premium is paid once at construction and the saving shows up as years of repair bills, closures and price cuts that never happen.

Recall

Q. In the composite parking deck case, what was the root cause?

A. A quality system that measured strength and ignored durability, so a mix above the water ratio limit, unrecorded site water and thin cover all passed unread.

Q. What is a lender's in-balance test?

A. The requirement that undisbursed loan plus remaining equity covers the full cost to complete before the lender funds the next draw.

Q. What is the difference between a roof's membrane and its insulation in control-layer terms?

A. The membrane is the water control layer, and often the air layer; the insulation is the thermal layer. They do different jobs and fail in different ways.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, value engineering sessions tend to look at durability items as cost lines with nothing visible behind them: a lower water ratio, a corrosion-inhibiting admixture, an extra half inch of cover, a deck coating, more curing time. Each one looks like money spent on something nobody will see. Today you learn to price both sides so you can defend those items with numbers, and drop the ones that do not earn their cost.

Pricing the premium

In plain English: a lower water ratio usually means more cementing material or more admixture per cubic yard, and that costs more.

Worked example, hypothetical round numbers. A building's exposed elements, such as parking decks, balconies and the podium roof, use 4,000 cubic yards of concrete. Moving from a 0.45 to a 0.40 mix adds about 8 dollars per cubic yard. A corrosion-inhibiting admixture adds 12 dollars per cubic yard. An extra half inch of cover on decks adds a little concrete and depth, say 20,000 dollars. A penetrating sealer on exposed decks costs 60,000 dollars. Total durability premium: 4,000 times 20, which is 80,000 dollars, plus 20,000 and 60,000, which is 160,000 dollars. On a 30,000,000 dollar project that is about half of one percent.

Pricing what it avoids

Now the other side. Suppose, from the engineer's judgment and from experience with similar structures, that without these measures a major corrosion repair becomes likely around year 12, costing 2,000,000 dollars, plus a parking closure that costs 150,000 dollars of lost income and resident concessions. With them, the major repair is pushed past year 25 or avoided within the holding horizon. These figures are hypothetical; real ones need an engineer's durability assessment.

To compare money at different times, discount it. At a hypothetical 7 percent discount rate, 1 dollar in 12 years is worth about 0.44 dollars today, because 1.07 to the power 12 is about 2.25. So 2,150,000 dollars in year 12 is worth about 950,000 dollars today. Even if you think the repair is only half as likely as stated, the expected present cost is about 475,000 dollars. A 160,000 dollar premium that removes a 475,000 dollar expected cost is a good trade.

Say that out loud now.

How the market reads it

The comparison above leaves out the larger effect: value. A building that is selling, refinancing or being appraised is examined by the buyer's or lender's engineer. A condition report that shows chloride contamination at steel depth, or spalling, leads to a price reduction or a repair escrow at least equal to the repair estimate, and often a risk discount on top, because buyers dislike open-ended problems. A clean report with documented mixes, cover and curing is the opposite: it removes a question. If net operating income, NOI, is 2,000,000 dollars and the market cap rate is 6 percent, value is about 33,300,000 dollars. A buyer who cuts 2,500,000 dollars for a deck repair and its risk has taken a sum far larger than the original premium, at the worst time.

Which items earn their cost

Not every durability item pays. An interior column in a dry, conditioned space faces no chlorides and little moisture; specifying it to a seafront exposure class wastes money. The discipline is location by location: classify exposure, apply measures where the exposure is real, and spend nothing extra where it is not. Ask the engineer for a durability schedule listing each element, its exposure class, its mix, its cover and any protective measure. That schedule is also what you will hand a buyer's engineer at sale.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note: a building is often the largest asset on a developer's personal balance sheet, directly or through an entity. Latent defects are a hidden liability against it. Durability spending converts an unknown future liability into a small known cost now, which makes the asset easier to borrow against, easier to sell and easier to pass on. For a personal balance sheet, a predictable asset is worth more than a cheaper unpredictable one. A licensed adviser is required before you act on how any asset is held or financed.

Worked example two: the repair in the pro forma

Now place the risk in the hold-period model, Mr Shabazz. Suppose you plan to hold for 10 years and sell. Without durability measures, the engineer expects visible distress by around year 8. A buyer's engineer in year 10 will find it. Hypothetically, the buyer prices a 2,000,000 dollar repair plus a 500,000 dollar risk discount, so your sale price falls by 2,500,000 dollars. Discounted at 7 percent from year 10, a factor of about 0.51, that is a loss of about 1,270,000 dollars in today's money, landing directly on your equity, because the lender's loan is repaid first from the sale.

Run the levered effect. If your equity in the deal is 9,000,000 dollars and the expected sale profit to equity is 8,000,000 dollars, a 2,500,000 dollar price cut removes nearly a third of the profit. Your internal rate of return falls by a meaningful amount for a defect that a 160,000 dollar premium would likely have avoided. Leverage magnifies the loss on equity, exactly as it magnifies gains. That is the strongest single argument you can put to a partner who wants the premium cut.

Where the money is wasted

The honest counterpart is that durability spending can also be wasted. Corrosion inhibitors in dry interior slabs, seafront mixes in fully conditioned basements, and extra cover where fire and durability requirements are already met by a thinner section add cost without benefit. A durability schedule exposes those as clearly as it exposes the gaps.

So the full discipline has three steps. Classify every element. Price the measure and the avoided cost, discounted, including the effect at exit. Then keep the measures that pay and drop the ones that do not, in writing, with the engineer's agreement. A partner who sees that process will trust both your additions and your cuts, because each one carries its own arithmetic and its own signature.

One caution on the inputs. The likelihood and timing of a future repair are judgments, not measurements. Ask the engineer for a range rather than a single year, run the comparison at both ends, and see whether the decision changes. If the premium wins even at the optimistic end, the decision is robust. If it wins only at the pessimistic end, you have a genuine judgment to make, and you should say so to your partners rather than present the number as certain.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a value engineering cut that removes durability measures from exposed elements because their benefit is invisible on the day. The control is a durability schedule by element, priced both ways, reviewed by the engineer before any cut.

The beginner's mistake

Comparing a premium today with a repair cost in year 12 without discounting, which overstates the case, or ignoring value at exit, which understates it. Do both.

Callback

In Week 107, Zara and Quincy taught life-cycle cost: compare options over their life, not their first cost. Durability is the cleanest example. The concrete premium is a first cost; the repair, closure and value loss are life-cycle costs that only a long view sees.

Recap

A durability premium on exposed concrete is a small share of project cost. Discounting shows its avoided repair is usually worth more today. Value at exit adds a further, larger reason. Spend where exposure is real, nowhere else.

Next: Ivo, on The Rules: what ACI and ASTM require of concrete materials and testing.
checklist: I have a durability schedule listing each element's exposure class, mix and cover.
I price durability items both as a premium now and as an avoided cost later.
I discount future repair costs to today before comparing.
I consider the effect of a condition report on value at exit.
I spend durability premiums only where exposure is real.
No durability measure is cut without the engineer's review.
I keep the durability records ready for a buyer's or lender's engineer.
Professional sign-off required: structural engineer for the durability assessment.
head: Field checklist
speak: Durability is cheap value protection. In a hypothetical building, 4,000 cubic yards of exposed concrete cost about 20 dollars more per yard for a lower water ratio and a corrosion inhibitor, plus extra cover and a sealer: about 160,000 dollars, half a percent of a 30,000,000 dollar project. Without them, suppose a 2,150,000 dollar repair and closure becomes likely around year 12. At 7 percent, that is worth about 950,000 today, and even at half the likelihood, about 475,000. So the premium wins. Then add value: a buyer's engineer who finds chlorides at the steel cuts the price by more than the repair. The discipline is location by location: classify exposure, spend where it is real, and nowhere else, with a durability schedule I can hand a buyer.
terms: Durability schedule — a list of each concrete element with its exposure class, mix, cover and any protective measure.
Discount rate — the annual rate used to convert future money into its value today.
Corrosion-inhibiting admixture — a chemical added to concrete to delay corrosion of embedded steel by chlorides.

hostile.q: I'm the value engineering consultant. The corrosion inhibitor and the lower water ratio cost 80,000 dollars and nobody will ever see them. Why keep them?
hostile.a: Because they are not invisible to the buyer's engineer, the lender at refinance or the residents when a deck closes. On the exposed elements only, they cost about 80,000 dollars. The engineer's assessment puts a major corrosion repair around year 12 without them, worth roughly half a million dollars today even at half the likelihood, before any price cut at sale. I am happy to drop them from interior elements where the exposure is not real, and I would like your help finding those.

title: The Rules in the Mix: ACI, ASTM and Acceptance
summary: The concrete code assigns exposure categories and their limits, a reference specification sets how concrete is produced and placed, and ASTM standards define how it is sampled and tested. Strength acceptance follows defined criteria, and a low result triggers an investigation, not an argument. Know where each rule lives and who must sign.
body:
Concrete is governed by three layers of rules, the code that sets limits by exposure, the specification that sets how concrete is made and placed, and the test standards that say how it is proven, and a low break is a defined process under those rules rather than a negotiation.

Recall

Q. Why discount a future repair cost before comparing it with a durability premium?

A. Because money in the future is worth less than money today, so an undiscounted comparison overstates the benefit of spending now.

Q. What does ASTM D1143 cover?

A. Static axial compressive load testing of deep foundation elements: loading a pile with jacks against a reaction and measuring its movement. Confirm the current edition.

Q. Why does airtightness matter in a hot-humid envelope?

A. Air leaks carry humid outdoor air into cool cavities, where moisture condenses and causes mould and decay, so the air control layer must be continuous.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, when a cylinder breaks low or a supplier proposes a substitute mix, the conversation turns quickly to who is right. Knowing where each rule lives lets you move it back to what the documents say and what evidence settles it. You do not need to memorise numbers. You need to know which document governs and who must sign.

Layer one: the code

In plain English: the code says what kind of concrete each part of the building needs, based on what it will face.

ACI 318, Building Code Requirements for Structural Concrete, published by the American Concrete Institute, is referenced by the International Building Code for structural concrete. It sets durability requirements by exposure category. In recent editions those categories cover freezing and thawing, sulfate exposure, conditions requiring low permeability in contact with water, and corrosion protection of reinforcement, each with classes of increasing severity [unverified — confirm independently]. For each class it sets limits such as maximum w/cm, minimum specified strength and, for some classes, limits on chlorides in the mix or air content. It also sets minimum cover for reinforcement depending on the element and its exposure. Verify every limit against the current adopted edition of ACI 318 and any local amendments; the edition your jurisdiction adopted may not be the latest.

Layer two: the specification

The project specification turns the code into instructions. Many specifications reference ACI 301, Specifications for Concrete Construction, which covers submittals, production, delivery, placing, curing, tolerances and testing. Ready-mixed concrete delivery is commonly governed by ASTM C94, which covers how concrete is ordered, batched and delivered, including tickets [unverified — confirm independently]. The specification tells the supplier and the contractor what records to produce, what limits on temperature and time from batching apply, and who may authorise water or admixture at site. If your specification is silent on any of those, you have a gap to close before the first pour.

Say that out loud now.

Layer three: sampling and testing

ASTM standards define the tests. Sampling fresh concrete follows ASTM C172. Slump, a simple measure of how stiff fresh concrete is, follows ASTM C143. Concrete temperature follows ASTM C1064. Air content, where air entrainment is specified, has its own methods. Cylinders are made and cured in the field under ASTM C31 and broken in the laboratory under ASTM C39. Confirm current editions and which ones your specification calls up.

The code also defines how strength is accepted. Under ACI 318, a strength test is generally the average of at least two cylinders from the same sample, broken at the specified age, and strength is commonly accepted when the average of any three consecutive tests meets or exceeds the specified strength and no single test falls below it by more than a defined margin [unverified — confirm independently]. Verify the exact criteria in the adopted edition.

Worked example: is this a low break?

Hypothetical round numbers. Specified strength is 5,000 psi. Five consecutive 28-day tests read 5,400, 5,100, 4,600, 4,800 and 5,300 psi. Check running averages of three: 5,400, 5,100 and 4,600 average 5,033; 5,100, 4,600 and 4,800 average 4,833, below 5,000; 4,600, 4,800 and 5,300 average 4,900, also below. Individual tests: the lowest, 4,600, is 400 below specified. Under a criterion that allows an individual test to fall 500 psi below specified strength, no single test fails, but two running averages do. The concrete is not automatically defective, but the acceptance criterion is not met and an investigation is triggered.

What an investigation looks like

A low result starts a defined sequence. First, check the testing: were cylinders made, handled, cured and capped correctly? Field cylinders left in the sun or bounced in a truck break low for reasons that say nothing about the structure. Second, the structural engineer checks whether the lower strength still satisfies the design, since many elements have margin. Third, if needed, in-place testing, such as cores drilled from the structure and tested under the governing standard, with their own acceptance criteria. Fourth, if the concrete still does not satisfy the design, remediation is designed by the engineer. Professional sign-off required: structural engineer of record. The sequence is evidence first, argument never.

Worked example: the substitution request

A supplier proposes replacing 25 percent of the cement with fly ash, at the same total cementing content and the same w/cm. Fly ash, a by-product of coal combustion, can improve workability, lower heat and reduce permeability over time, but it slows early strength gain, which matters for stripping forms and for cold weather. The rule is not that substitution is bad. It is that the structural engineer reviews the submittal against the exposure limits, the early-strength needs of the schedule and any limits the code places on supplementary materials in certain exposures, and approves it in writing before it is used.

What the owner keeps

The rules create records, and the owner should keep a full set. For every pour: the approved mix submittal with the engineer's stamp, the batch tickets for every truck, the inspector's pre-pour and placement reports, the field test results for slump, temperature and air where specified, the cylinder identification log and every laboratory report, including the individual results behind any summary. Index them by pour location and date, so that any element in the building can be traced to its concrete in minutes.

Two reasons matter, Mr Shabazz. During construction, the records let you run the acceptance check yourself and see a trend before it becomes a dispute, for instance a slow slide in running averages from one supplier plant. After construction, they are what a buyer's engineer, an insurer or a court will ask for. Concrete has a long memory, and so should your file.

Hot and cold rules

Two more references sit behind most specifications. ACI 305 covers hot-weather concreting and ACI 306 covers cold-weather concreting. Both are guides that a specification adopts by reference or adapts. They address material temperatures, protection, admixtures and curing. If your site is hot most of the year, the hot-weather provisions are not occasional; they are the normal operating rules, and the specification should say so plainly.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a specification gap, such as no rule on site water or no maximum temperature, that leaves every argument on site to whoever is loudest. The control is to read the concrete specification against this list before the pre-construction meeting.

The beginner's mistake

Calling one low cylinder a failure. Acceptance is defined over tests and averages, and a low break starts an investigation.

Callback

Yesterday Sage priced durability. Today's rules are where that price comes from: the exposure category sets the w/cm and strength limits, and the cover rule sets the extra depth. The money and the code are one decision.

Recap

ACI 318 sets exposure limits and acceptance criteria. The specification, often referencing ACI 301 and ASTM C94, governs production and placement. ASTM methods govern sampling and testing. A low break starts a defined investigation, signed off by the engineer.

Next: Ingrid, on The Numbers: reverse engineering a mix from the strength it must reach.
checklist: I know which edition of ACI 318 my jurisdiction has adopted.
Each element's exposure category and class is stated in the drawings or specification.
The specification covers site water, temperature, time limits and who authorises changes.
I know which ASTM methods govern sampling, slump, temperature and cylinders.
I can apply the running average and individual acceptance checks.
A low result triggers a written investigation sequence.
Substitutions need the structural engineer's written approval.
Professional sign-off required: structural engineer of record and testing laboratory.
head: Field checklist
speak: Concrete is governed in three layers. The code, ACI 318, sets durability limits by exposure category, such as maximum water ratio and minimum strength, plus cover and acceptance criteria; I verify every limit against the adopted edition. The specification, often referencing ACI 301 and ASTM C94, governs submittals, delivery, placing, curing and who may add water. ASTM methods govern sampling, slump, temperature and cylinders, made under C31 and broken under C39. Acceptance looks at averages of three consecutive tests and at how far any single test falls short. In a hypothetical run against 5,000 psi, two running averages of 4,833 and 4,900 miss even though no single test is far below. That starts an investigation: check the testing, check the design margin, take cores if needed, and let the engineer decide.
terms: Strength test — the average strength of at least two cylinders from one sample of concrete, broken at the specified age.
Slump — a simple field measure of how stiff fresh concrete is, the drop of a cone of concrete when the mould is lifted.
Supplementary cementitious material — fly ash, slag cement, silica fume or similar material used with or in place of some portland cement.

hostile.q: I'm the concrete supplier. Your 28-day results averaged under 5,000 for two sets. My plant data is fine. Are you really going to hold back payment?
hostile.a: I am not holding back on an argument; I am following the specification. The acceptance criterion is not met, so we investigate. First, our laboratory reviews the handling and curing of those cylinders, and I would welcome your plant data alongside it. Second, the structural engineer checks the design margin for those pours. If that does not settle it, cores are taken under the governing standard. If the cores pass, the concrete is accepted and you are paid in full. If not, the engineer designs the remedy and the contract decides who pays.

title: Reverse Engineering a Mix From the Strength It Must Reach
summary: Start from the finished outcome, a specified strength and an exposure class, and work backward to the average strength the mix must reach, the water ratio that delivers it, and the water and cement per cubic yard. Then run it forward to see what site water does to the result. Hypothetical round numbers throughout.
body:
Work backward from the strength the engineer specified and the exposure the concrete faces, and you arrive at the exact amount of water the mix can hold, which is why one extra bucket at site is not a detail but a departure from the design.

Recall

Q. Under the typical acceptance approach, what two checks are applied to strength tests?

A. The average of three consecutive tests must meet the specified strength, and no single test may fall below it by more than a defined margin. Verify the exact criteria in the adopted edition.

Q. In a pile calculation, why do you round the pile count up?

A. Because capacity cannot be shared between columns; 8.08 piles means 9 piles.

Q. In a hot-humid climate, which way does vapour usually drive through a wall?

A. From the hot, humid outside toward the cooler, drier conditioned inside.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is an even week, so we start from the finished outcome and work backward. You will never design a mix, but if you can rebuild the chain from specified strength to water per cubic yard, you will see immediately why a supplier's substitution, a hot day or a pump problem can change the concrete in your building. All numbers are hypothetical round figures in American units. Pounds per square inch is psi; a cubic yard is about 0.76 cubic metres.

Step 1: the outcome

The structural engineer specifies a podium deck exposed to de-icing salt from vehicles: specified strength 5,000 psi at 28 days, and a corrosion exposure class whose limit, in our hypothetical specification, is a maximum w/cm of 0.40. The w/cm limit is a durability requirement. The strength is a structural requirement. The mix must satisfy both.

Step 2: from specified to required average strength

Concrete varies truck to truck. If the mix averaged exactly 5,000 psi, about half the tests would fall below it. So the mix must be proportioned to a higher average, called the required average compressive strength, enough above specified strength that low tests are rare.

The concrete code gives formulas that use the supplier's measured standard deviation, a statistic describing how widely its results scatter. For specified strengths up to 5,000 psi, a common form takes the larger of two values: specified strength plus 1.34 times the standard deviation, and specified strength plus 2.33 times the standard deviation, minus 500 psi [unverified — confirm independently]. Verify against the current adopted edition of ACI 318.

Our supplier's records show a standard deviation of 500 psi. First value: 5,000 plus 1.34 times 500, which is 5,000 plus 670, giving 5,670 psi. Second value: 5,000 plus 2.33 times 500, which is 1,165, minus 500, giving 5,665 psi. The larger is 5,670 psi. The mix must average about 5,670 psi.

A supplier with no history must use a larger fixed margin, which the code tabulates. A consistent supplier earns a smaller margin and a cheaper mix. Consistency is worth money.

Say that out loud now.

Step 3: from average strength to water ratio

The supplier's trial batches, made with your actual cement, sand, stone and admixtures, show a relationship between w/cm and 28-day strength. In our hypothetical data: 0.45 gives 5,200 psi, 0.40 gives 5,900 psi, 0.35 gives 6,700 psi. To reach 5,670 psi, the strength line alone would allow about 0.42. The exposure limit says 0.40. Take the stricter: 0.40, giving an expected average around 5,900 psi, comfortably above 5,670. Here, durability governs, not strength. That is common in exposed concrete, and it is the reason a mix that meets strength can still fail the specification.

Step 4: from water ratio to water and cement

With the chosen stone size and a water-reducing admixture, the mix needs about 270 pounds of water per cubic yard to reach the specified slump. Cementing material is water divided by w/cm: 270 divided by 0.40, which is 675 pounds per cubic yard. If 20 percent of that is slag cement, the mix holds 540 pounds of portland cement and 135 of slag. Sand, stone and air make up the rest of the cubic yard.

Run it forward: what one addition does

Now the truck reaches site and the pump operator wants it wetter. The driver adds 8 gallons. At about 8.34 pounds a gallon, that is about 67 pounds of water. Water becomes 337 pounds, and w/cm becomes 337 divided by 675, which is about 0.50. From the trial batch line, 0.50 sits below the 0.45 point at 5,200 psi, so strength drops toward perhaps 4,500 psi, under the 5,000 psi specified, and the deck is now well outside its 0.40 durability limit.

Some specifications allow water to be added at site up to the amount withheld at the plant, so long as the approved w/cm is never exceeded. If the plant batched with 20 pounds withheld, only that 20 pounds, about 2.4 gallons, may go in, recorded on the ticket. Every gallon past that is outside the design.

Reverse engineering a low result

One more backward step. A set of cylinders from one pour averages 4,600 psi, against an expected 5,900. Reading the trial batch line backward, 4,600 psi corresponds to roughly 0.49 to 0.50 w/cm. Pull that pour's batch tickets. If they show water added, you have a likely explanation and a durability question as well as a strength one. If they show nothing, look at sampling, curing and the laboratory. Either way, the engineer evaluates the in-place concrete. Professional sign-off required: structural engineer of record.

Worked example two: pricing consistency

Run the margin arithmetic for a second supplier, Mr Shabazz. This one has a standard deviation of 700 psi. The first formula gives 5,000 plus 1.34 times 700, which is 5,000 plus 938, or 5,938 psi. The second gives 5,000 plus 2.33 times 700, which is 1,631, minus 500, giving 6,131 psi. The larger is 6,131 psi. To reach it, the trial batch line points to a w/cm of roughly 0.38, below the 0.40 durability limit, so here strength governs instead, and the mix needs more cementing material: 270 divided by 0.38 is about 711 pounds per cubic yard, against 675 for the consistent supplier.

That is 36 extra pounds of cementing material per cubic yard. At a hypothetical 0.10 dollars a pound, it is 3.60 dollars a yard, or about 10,800 dollars on 3,000 cubic yards, before the added heat and shrinkage that richer mixes bring. The cheaper quote per yard from an inconsistent supplier may not be cheaper once the margin is applied. Ask every supplier for its standard deviation and the number of tests behind it, and compare mixes at the required average strength, not at the specified one.

Put both suppliers on one line for the decision log: specified strength, standard deviation, required average strength, governing limit, w/cm, cementing material per cubic yard and delivered price at that content. The comparison takes ten minutes and often reverses the ranking of the quotes. It also shows the supplier with the better record that consistency is what you are paying for, which is the behaviour you want to reward.

Keep the trial batch data with the decision. If results drift later, you will need to know which relationship between water ratio and strength the mix was designed on, and the supplier's sales sheet will not tell you.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a mix that meets strength but not its exposure limit, because strength is what everyone checks. The control is to ask, for every mix, which limit governs, strength or durability, and to check the w/cm on the submittal against it.

The beginner's mistake

Treating specified strength as the target average. The mix must average higher, by a margin set by the supplier's consistency.

Callback

In Week 17, Sage taught reverse engineering a deal: start from the price and work backward to the implied land value and rent. Today's method is the same. Start from what the building must achieve and work back to what the truck may contain, and every departure becomes visible.

Recap

Specified strength plus a variability margin gives required average strength. Trial batches give the w/cm for that strength. The exposure limit may be stricter and then governs. Water and w/cm give cement content. A few gallons at site can push the mix outside both limits.

Next: Ingrid, on The Room: the supplier meeting about a substitute mix.
checklist: I know the specified strength and exposure limit for each mix.
I ask the supplier for its standard deviation and how many tests support it.
I check the required average strength the mix was proportioned for.
I ask whether strength or durability governs the w/cm.
I know how much water, if any, the plant withholds for site addition.
Site water is limited to the withheld amount and recorded on the ticket.
Low results are traced back through batch tickets and testing records.
Professional sign-off required: structural engineer of record.
head: Field checklist
speak: I start from the outcome and work back. A podium deck is specified at 5,000 psi with a durability limit of 0.40 water ratio. Concrete varies, so the mix must average higher: with a supplier standard deviation of 500 psi, the code's formulas give about 5,670 psi. Trial batches show 0.42 would reach that, but the exposure limit says 0.40, so durability governs, giving about 5,900 psi. At 270 pounds of water, 0.40 means 675 pounds of cementing material per cubic yard. Then I run it forward: 8 gallons added at site is about 67 pounds of water, taking the ratio to about 0.50 and strength toward 4,500 psi, outside both limits. So site water is limited to what the plant withheld and recorded on the ticket, and a low break is traced back through the tickets.
terms: Required average compressive strength — the average strength a mix must be proportioned to reach so that tests rarely fall below specified strength.
Standard deviation — a statistic describing how widely a supplier's test results scatter around their average.
Trial batch — a test mix made with the project's actual materials to establish the relationship between water ratio and strength.

hostile.q: I'm the ready-mix supplier. My mix hits 5,000 easily at 0.45. Why are you forcing me to 0.40 and costing me cement?
hostile.a: Because strength is not the only requirement on this deck. The engineer classified it for corrosion exposure from de-icing salts, and the specification limits it to 0.40 for durability, so durability governs, not strength. Your 0.45 mix would pass the cylinders and fail the specification. If you can show me a 0.40 mix using slag or another approved material that keeps your cost down, submit it with trial batch data and the engineer will review it.

title: The Supplier Meeting About a Substitute Mix
summary: The ready-mix supplier wants to substitute a cheaper mix for the exposed decks, the contractor wants the saving, and the structural engineer has not seen it yet. The lesson is how to hold the line on what the specification protects, find what is negotiable, and leave with a written decision. Closes with this month's thread on working with advisers.
body:
In a substitution meeting the owner's job is to separate what the specification protects, which is not for sale, from how it is achieved, which often is, and to make sure the engineer, not the room, decides.

Recall

Q. If a mix has 675 pounds of cementing material and 270 pounds of water, what is its w/cm, and what does adding 67 pounds of water do?

A. 0.40, rising to about 0.50, which typically lowers strength and puts the mix outside a 0.40 durability limit.

Q. What is a hold point?

A. A stage beyond which work may not proceed until a named party approves in writing.

Q. What is the main risk of a value engineering session on an envelope?

A. Removing or substituting a control layer component, such as a membrane or flashing, whose performance nobody in the room can see, without the designer's review.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, substitution requests arrive at the moment of maximum pressure: procurement is late, a supplier is cheaper, and the contractor has a saving to share. Most substitutions are honest and some are better. A few quietly trade away the thing the specification exists to protect. You need to tell them apart in the room without pretending to be a materials engineer.

The scene

Hypothetical. The exposed podium decks are specified at 5,000 psi with a 0.40 maximum w/cm and a corrosion-inhibiting admixture. A new supplier offers a mix at 0.45 with no inhibitor, at 18 dollars less per cubic yard on 3,000 cubic yards, a 54,000 dollar saving. The contractor proposes splitting it. The supplier's representative says the mix has been used on many projects. The structural engineer's office has not received the submittal. Your quality manager is present.

The question behind the question

The contractor asks, "Can we approve this today?" The question behind it is: will you accept the schedule risk if you say no, and can I keep my supplier? The supplier asks, "Is price the only issue?" The question behind it is: what would make my product acceptable? That second question is an opening. Take it.

The lines to say

Open with the frame. "The specification protects two things on these decks: strength and resistance to salt. Strength is 5,000 psi. Salt resistance is the 0.40 limit and the inhibitor. Those two outcomes are not negotiable. How you reach them often is."

To the supplier: "If you can meet 0.40 and the corrosion protection with your materials, perhaps with slag cement or another approved option instead of the inhibitor, submit it with trial batch data. The engineer will review it against the exposure class."

To the contractor: "Nothing is approved in this room. The submittal goes to the structural engineer, and I will ask for a review within a set number of days so the schedule holds. If it is rejected, we use the specified mix."

Say that out loud now.

A worked trade

Hypothetical. The supplier returns with a mix at 0.40 using 30 percent slag cement, which lowers permeability over time, and proposes to drop the inhibitor. Price: 6 dollars less per cubic yard than the specified mix, an 18,000 dollar saving. The engineer reviews it and accepts the slag mix but keeps the inhibitor on the deck areas nearest the vehicle entry, where salt load is heaviest, about a third of the volume, while allowing it to be omitted elsewhere. Net saving: about 12,000 dollars after the inhibitor on 1,000 cubic yards. A smaller saving than 54,000 dollars, but a real one, with the protection intact, and the engineer's name on it.

One more check. Slag slows early strength gain, which affects when forms can be stripped. Ask the contractor to confirm the stripping and reshoring plan still works, or the saving disappears into a slower floor cycle.

The lines never to say

"If it hits strength, it's fine." That sentence approves the defect in the composite parking deck case.

"Let's split the saving and move on." Agreeing a commercial split before a technical approval tells everyone the technical review is a formality.

"I trust you." Trust is not the issue. The engineer's stamp is.

When to stay silent

After you state that the two outcomes are not negotiable, stop. The supplier will either defend price, which tells you the mix cannot meet them, or ask what would work, which tells you it can. Your silence lets them choose, and their choice tells you more than any data sheet.

Holding your state

Pressure in this meeting comes from the schedule, not from the concrete. Name the schedule question openly so it stops driving the room: "The real worry is the date. Here is how the review keeps the date." Then speak slowly. You do not need to win the technical point, only to route it to the person who must decide.

Monthly thread: working with advisers

This meeting shows the right use of an adviser. You did not ask the structural engineer to attend and approve on the spot, and you did not decide yourself. You framed the question, sent it in writing, set a deadline and accepted the answer, including the part you did not want. Good advisers do their best work when the owner defines the question, gives them the evidence and does not lead them toward the cheap answer.

The opposite habit is common and costly: ringing an adviser for a quick yes, or shopping for an opinion that matches what you already decided. Over a career, Mr Shabazz, the developers who get the best advice are the ones advisers trust to use it honestly. Ask yourself after each such meeting whether you asked a question or requested a permission.

After the meeting

Within the day, send a short note: what the specification protects, the alternative invited, the date the submittal is due, the date the engineer's review is due, and the fact that the specified mix remains the default if the review is not complete before the pour. Copy the quality manager and the inspector, so that nobody on site treats the proposed mix as approved by rumour. When the engineer's review arrives, issue it to the supplier, the contractor and the testing laboratory, because the laboratory needs to know which mix it is testing against.

Then check the first trucks of any approved substitute closely: tickets, slump, temperature and cylinders, and a quick look at early-age strength results if the engineer asked for them. A new mix is a new risk until its first few pours confirm it behaves as its trial batches promised.

A final note on relationships. The supplier who offered the cheaper mix is not an adversary. It made a commercial proposal, and you answered it on the merits with a path to yes. Suppliers remember owners who are firm on outcomes and fair on methods, and those are the owners who hear first about better materials, tighter plant control and capacity when the market is busy. Firmness and fairness together are a competitive advantage in procurement, not a softness.

Write the outcome in the minutes in neutral language: what was proposed, what was approved, why, and what was not. Neutral minutes are the ones every party signs without argument, and signed minutes are the ones that settle disputes later.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a substitution approved in the room on commercial grounds before technical review. The control is a written rule: no substitution without the engineer's written approval, and no commercial split agreed until then.

The beginner's mistake

Rejecting every substitution on reflex. Some are better, and a supplier who is never heard stops offering improvements.

Callback

In Week 66, Kema and JAX taught the difference between interests and positions. The supplier's position was a cheaper mix; its interest was keeping the order. Separating the two is what turned a refusal into a trade that protected the decks.

Recap

State what the specification protects and treat it as fixed. Invite a compliant alternative. Route the decision to the engineer with a deadline. Check knock-on effects such as early strength. Record the decision.

Next: Kema, on Quiz and Recap: Week 112 review, with Cole's Auditor's Chair.
checklist: I state what the specification protects before discussing price.
I invite a compliant alternative instead of refusing outright.
No substitution is approved in the meeting.
The submittal goes to the structural engineer with a review deadline.
No commercial split is agreed before technical approval.
I check knock-on effects such as early strength and the stripping plan.
I record the decision and the engineer's approval in the decision log.
Professional sign-off required: structural engineer of record.
head: Field checklist
speak: In a substitution meeting I separate the outcome from the method. The specification on these decks protects strength, 5,000 psi, and salt resistance, the 0.40 water ratio and the corrosion inhibitor. Those are fixed. How the supplier reaches them is negotiable. So I invite a compliant alternative with trial batch data, and I say nothing is approved in the room: the submittal goes to the structural engineer with a deadline that protects the schedule. In a hypothetical case, the supplier came back with a 0.40 slag mix, the engineer kept the inhibitor near the vehicle entry and dropped it elsewhere, and we saved about 12,000 dollars with protection intact. I never say if it hits strength it's fine, and I check that slower early strength does not break the stripping plan.
terms: Substitution request — a contractor or supplier's formal proposal to use a material or product different from the one specified.
Slag cement — a by-product of iron production used as a supplementary cementing material, which can lower permeability but slows early strength.
Submittal review — the designer's formal check of a contractor's proposed product or mix against the contract documents.

hostile.q: I'm the general contractor. You're throwing away a 54,000 dollar saving and risking the pour date over an engineer's paperwork.
hostile.a: I am not throwing it away; I am routing it. The saving depended on dropping the water limit and the inhibitor that protect these decks from salt, and the specification does not let either of us trade those. If the supplier can meet them another way, the engineer reviews it within the deadline I have asked for, and the pour date holds. If the saving can be had honestly, I want it as much as you do.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 112 Review: The Recipe and the Evidence
summary: Six questions on concrete materials, a recap of the week, Cole's Auditor's Chair on a hypothetical mix submittal and test report, and a two-minute boardroom drill with a model answer.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: concrete is only as good as the water ratio, the exposure limits and the cover it actually received, so the owner's job is to insist on evidence for all three, not just a strength report.

Recall

Q. In the substitution meeting, what was fixed and what was negotiable?

A. The outcomes the specification protects, strength and salt resistance, were fixed. The method of reaching them, such as the supplier's materials, was negotiable, subject to the engineer's approval.

Q. What is the purpose of an indicator pile?

A. To confirm the pile design with the production rig and a load test before production piling starts.

Q. What is a field test of a window installation meant to prove?

A. That the installed window and its connection to the wall resist water, and often air, as specified, under defined pressure, before the work is closed in.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, if you can answer these six without notes, you can sit with a supplier, a testing laboratory and a structural engineer and follow every number. Answer each aloud first.

The six questions

Question 1. What does the water-cementitious ratio measure, and why does lower usually mean better?

Answer: Water weight divided by the weight of cement and supplementary materials. Less excess water means fewer pores, so higher strength and lower permeability.

Question 2. What does an exposure class do?

Answer: It tells the code what the concrete will face, such as freezing, sulfate, water or chlorides, and sets limits such as maximum w/cm and minimum strength.

Question 3. What was the root cause in the composite parking deck case?

Answer: A quality system that measured strength and ignored durability: an over-limit mix, unrecorded site water and thin cover, all of which passed unread.

Question 4. Why must a mix average above its specified strength?

Answer: Because concrete varies, and a mix averaging exactly the specified strength would fail about half its tests. The margin depends on the supplier's consistency.

Question 5. What happens after a strength test misses its acceptance criterion?

Answer: An investigation: check the testing, check the design margin, take cores if needed, and let the engineer decide on any remedy.

Question 6. A mix with 600 pounds of cementing material and 240 pounds of water has 6 gallons added. What is the new w/cm?

Answer: Six gallons is about 50 pounds. Water is 290 pounds; 290 divided by 600 is about 0.48, up from 0.40.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Ingrid framed concrete as a recipe with a contract attached. Ford and Cole took a composite coastal parking deck through seven steps, giving Rule 112. Sage priced durability both ways. Ivo set out ACI 318, the specification and the ASTM tests. Ingrid reverse engineered a mix. Ingrid ran the substitution meeting.

Cole's Auditor's Chair

Week 112 is a fourth week, so the Red Pen becomes Cole's Auditor's Chair: read this hypothetical mix submittal and test summary as a hostile auditor would. Find the defects before reading on.

Mix submittal M-3, podium decks, corrosion exposure. Specified strength 5,000 psi. Proposed w/cm 0.44. Supplier standard deviation: not available; proportioned for 5,600 psi average. Corrosion inhibitor: omitted, per supplier experience. Reviewed: contractor's project manager, approved. Site water: may be added as required for placement. Test summary, pours 1 to 6: all cylinders exceed 5,000 psi at 28 days. Cylinders cured on site in the contractor's trailer.

The defects. First, a w/cm of 0.44 on a deck whose exposure class limits it lower is non-compliant on its face, whatever its strength. Second, with no standard deviation the code requires a larger fixed margin, and the submittal does not show it was applied. Third, the inhibitor is omitted on supplier experience, not on the engineer's decision. Fourth, it was approved by the contractor's project manager rather than the structural engineer of record. Fifth, site water as required is an open door to the parking deck failure. Sixth, a summary saying all cylinders exceed 5,000 psi hides the individual results and running averages that acceptance actually uses. Seventh, cylinders cured in a trailer may not meet standard curing, so the results themselves are questionable.

Then the auditor asks for the evidence: the engineer's stamped review, the exposure classification for each deck, trial batch data, the supplier's test history, every batch ticket for pours 1 to 6, the individual test results, and the laboratory's curing records. A submittal that cannot produce those in an hour was approved on hope.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, to a partner who asks, "Why do we fuss about concrete if the cylinders pass?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Cylinders prove the strength of the concrete that was sampled. They do not prove its durability or what happened after sampling. Durability depends mainly on the water ratio, which the code limits by exposure, and on the cover over the steel. A mix can pass strength and still fail the water limit, and water added at the truck makes it worse while the samples, taken earlier, look fine. So we control four things: the engineer approves every mix against its exposure class, no water goes in at site beyond what the mix allows and every addition is on the ticket, cover is measured before each pour, and curing is specified and recorded. It costs well under one percent and protects us from repairs that cost millions and from price cuts when we sell."

Score your answer: bottom line first, the four controls named, the gap between cylinders and durability explained, inside two minutes. If not, record it again tomorrow.

Self-test before you move on

Kema's check, Mr Shabazz. On a card, without looking back, write the chain from a finished building back to the truck: exposure class, w/cm limit, required average strength, trial batch, water per cubic yard, cementing material per cubic yard, withheld water, batch ticket. Then write the four controls from the boardroom drill. Then Rule 112 in your own words. If you can do all three in two minutes, the week has landed.

Then one exercise for the next real project you look at. Ask for one batch ticket and one cylinder report from any pour, and read both line by line. Find the w/cm or the water added, the time from batching to placement, the concrete temperature, and the individual cylinder results. If you cannot find any of them on the documents, you have learned what the project is not recording, and that is the first question to ask its team. Reading two pieces of paper slowly teaches more than any summary, and it is the habit that would have saved the parking deck in this week's case.

Finally, link this week to the next. Concrete materials end at the chute. Everything after that, the placing, the vibration, the finishing, the curing, the forms and the shores, decides whether a good mix becomes good concrete in the structure. Next week Duke takes over in the field, and the same rule applies: evidence at every step, recorded on the day.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is a report that says passed and hides what was never tested. The control is to read the evidence, not the summary.

The beginner's mistake

Remembering 0.40 and 5,000 psi as rules. They are this week's hypothetical numbers. What you keep is the chain from exposure to w/cm to water on the truck.

Callback

In Week 83, Cole taught that audit means asking for the evidence behind each statement. Today's Auditor's Chair applied that to a single page: every line of the submittal either had evidence behind it or did not.

Recap

Water ratio, exposure class and cover set durability. The mix averages above specified strength. Acceptance is defined over tests, and a miss starts an investigation. Substitutions need the engineer. Rule 112 makes durability evidence a condition of every pour.

head: The six questions
speak: This week, concrete materials. Strength and durability are set mainly by the water-cementitious ratio, and the code limits it by exposure class, such as salt. Cover protects the steel. A mix must average above its specified strength by a margin set by the supplier's consistency, and in exposed concrete the durability limit often governs, not strength. Cylinders prove the sampled concrete, not water added later, cover or curing. The composite parking deck passed its cylinders and rusted, which gave Rule 112: no pour without evidence of the approved water ratio, exposure class and measured cover, and no unrecorded water at site. Durability costs well under one percent and protects value. A low break starts an investigation, and substitutions go to the engineer. I read the evidence, never just the summary.
terms: Standard curing — keeping test cylinders at controlled temperature and moisture as the test standard requires, so results reflect the concrete rather than the storage.
Running average — the average of a set number of consecutive results, here three strength tests, used in acceptance.
Withheld water — water deliberately left out at the plant so a limited amount can be added at site without exceeding the approved ratio.

hostile.q: I'm the auditor for a lender. Your submittals show the contractor approved the deck mix. Who actually checked that the concrete is durable?
hostile.a: You have found a gap and I will not defend it. The contractor's project manager approved submittal M-3, which the specification does not allow. I have sent it to the structural engineer of record for formal review against the exposure class, with the trial batch data, the supplier's history, every batch ticket and the individual test results. Until that review is complete, no further deck pours proceed on that mix, and I will report the outcome, including any testing of the pours already made, in the next monitor's report.
